questions.questionText: Which plant organ is responsible for absorbing water and minerals from the soil?
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil through root hairs and anchor the plant in the ground.

questions.questionText: Xylem transports:

options.text: Water and minerals from roots to all parts

questions.explanation: Xylem vessels conduct water and dissolved mineral salts from roots upwards to stems and leaves.

questions.questionText: Phloem transports:
questions.explanation: Phloem transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) from photosynthetic leaves to all parts of the plant for energy and storage.

questions.questionText: The leaf is the primary site of:
questions.explanation: Leaves contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis and have stomata for gas exchange, making them the primary food production site.

questions.questionText: The stem's primary function is to:

options.text: Support the plant and transport substances

questions.explanation: The stem provides structural support for the plant and contains vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) for transporting water and nutrients.

questions.questionText: Stomata are found on:
questions.explanation: Stomata are tiny pores mainly on the lower surface of leaves that allow gas exchange (CO2 in, O2 out) and transpiration.

questions.questionText: Root hairs function to:

options.text: Increase surface area for water and mineral absorption

questions.explanation: Root hairs are thin extensions of root epidermal cells that greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals from soil.

questions.questionText: Transpiration pull is generated by:
questions.explanation: Transpiration pull is created when water evaporates from stomata, creating a negative pressure that pulls water up through the xylem.

questions.questionText: The spongy mesophyll layer in a leaf:

options.text: Has loosely arranged cells and air spaces for gas exchange
Is covered by a waxy cuticle

questions.explanation: Spongy mesophyll has loosely arranged cells with large air spaces that facilitate gas exchange and allow CO2 and O2 to circulate.

questions.questionText: Which tissue in the leaf is responsible for most photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Palisade mesophyll cells are tightly packed with many chloroplasts and receive most direct sunlight, making them the primary photosynthetic tissue.

questions.questionText: The cohesion-tension theory explains:

options.text: How water is pulled up through xylem
How minerals are absorbed by roots

questions.explanation: Cohesion (water molecules attract each other) and tension (negative pressure from transpiration) together pull water up through xylem.

questions.questionText: Vascular bundles in a stem contain:
questions.explanation: Vascular bundles contain both xylem (water transport) and phloem (food transport) tissues, plus cambium in some plants.

questions.questionText: Which cells control the opening and closing of stomata?
questions.explanation: Guard cells flank each stoma and control its opening and closing by changing shape in response to water availability and light.

questions.questionText: Root pressure is caused by:

options.text: Active pumping of minerals into xylem and osmotic water movement

questions.explanation: Root pressure develops when active transport pumps minerals into xylem vessels, causing water to follow osmotically and push sap upward.

questions.questionText: The pressure-flow hypothesis explains the mechanism of:
questions.explanation: The pressure-flow hypothesis states sugars are loaded into phloem at sources (leaves), creating osmotic pressure that pushes fluids to sinks (roots, fruits).

questions.questionText: When guard cells take up water and become turgid, the stomatal pore:
questions.explanation: When guard cells absorb water and become turgid, their curved shape pulls the stomatal pore open, allowing gas exchange.

questions.questionText: Which factor would most increase the rate of transpiration?
questions.explanation: High temperature increases evaporation, and low humidity creates a steep concentration gradient, both accelerating transpiration.

questions.questionText: Sieve tube elements in phloem differ from xylem vessel elements because sieve tubes:

options.text: Contain cytoplasm and are alive at maturity

questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements are living cells (though lacking a nucleus) that form tubes for sugar transport, assisted by companion cells. Xylem vessels are dead.

questions.questionText: Wilting in plants is primarily caused by:

options.text: Excess water in the cell vacuoles
Loss of turgor pressure due to insufficient water

questions.explanation: Wilting occurs when water loss through transpiration exceeds water uptake, causing cells to lose turgor pressure and the plant to droop.

questions.questionText: The Casparian strip in the endodermis of a root:

options.text: Allows free diffusion of water into xylem
Blocks apoplastic pathway, forcing water into symplastic pathway

questions.explanation: The Casparian strip is a waxy suberin band in endodermal cell walls that blocks the apoplastic pathway, forcing water and minerals through cell membranes for selective uptake.
